title: Grandma's Secret Garden
summary: Two bored siblings arrive to spend the summer in the countryside, until the wind moves the ivy and a little blue door appears that has been waiting for them for years.

scenes.text: The bus dropped Mateo and Lucía off in front of Grandma Rosa's house, at the end of a dirt road. The summer smelled of warm bread and freshly cut grass. Grandma opened the wooden door and hugged them so tightly that Lucía's hat went crooked. 'My grandchildren!' she said, and the whole house filled up with her laugh. Mateo looked around. There was no television. There was no tablet. There was not even any signal for the phone. 'So what do you actually do here?' he asked, dropping his backpack with a sigh. 'Here you look, you listen, and you wait,' answered Grandma, giving him a wink. Lucía walked along the hallway of cool tiles, and the walls echoed back her steps. Outside, the cicadas sang without stopping and the sun painted the curtains gold. Mateo thought that this summer was going to be the longest and most boring one of his whole life. He did not yet know how right he was, or in what a strange way.

The first two days went by as slowly as snails. Mateo counted the cracks in the ceiling. Lucía gave a name to every hen. On the third day, boredom pushed them to the back of the yard, where nobody ever went. There stood an old wall, long and tall, covered by ivy so thick that it looked like a green blanket. 'It is only a wall,' said Mateo. But then, down from the mountain, came a wind. Warm and curious, it moved the ivy as if the wall were breathing, and the whole yard filled with the soft sound of the leaves. Lucía stood very still. 'Mateo... there is something hollow back there.' She reached out and pushed. The ivy gave way a little. Behind it there was no stone: there was wood. Mateo's heart gave a strange jump, one he had not felt in a long time. He began pulling branches aside with both hands, fast, without thinking, while Lucía held the green blanket open so it could not close again.

Under the ivy something appeared that was just the right size for a child and for a grandmother. It was painted blue, although the blue had been flaking off for years, and it had an iron handle shaped like a leaf. 'Do you think it is locked?' whispered Lucía. Mateo turned the handle. At first nothing moved at all. He pushed with his shoulder, counted to three, and then, with one big shove, he opened the door. The hinges woke up from a ten-year nap with a long, slow creak. Cool air touched their faces. It smelled of earth, of damp wood, and of something sweet they could not name. 'Mateo,' said Lucía, grabbing his finger, 'shall we go in?' He swallowed and nodded his head. They stepped through together, ducking down a little. And on the other side, surrounded by high walls, was a place nobody had walked in for a very, very long time: a whole garden, hidden from the world, waiting for them in silence.

But the garden was not like the ones in storybooks. It was dry. The weeds came up to Lucía's waist and the rosebushes were grey sticks with thorns. In the middle, a stone fountain held old leaves instead of water. Everything was still, so still that they could hear one single lost bee. It was searching for a flower that no longer existed. 'It is dead,' said Mateo, and he felt a strange sadness, like when somebody else's toy breaks. Behind them the garden gate creaked. It was Grandma Rosa, wearing her apron, her eyes shining. She came closer and spoke in a whisper. 'So you found it. Your grandfather and I planted this garden a great many years ago. When he was gone, I could not come here anymore. And weeds do not wait for anybody.' She stood looking at the fountain for a long while, saying nothing. 'What if we wake it up?' asked Lucía. Grandma smiled slowly, as if that question had spent years waiting under the ivy.

The next morning, Grandma gave them two pairs of old gloves and a bucket. They worked all week. They pulled weeds until their arms ached, gathered stones and swept up dry leaves. When the soil was finally bare and dark, Grandma taught them how to sow. 'With your finger, like this. A small hole. The seed inside. You cover it with love, not with strength.' Mateo looked at the seed in his hand: it was the size of a bread crumb. 'And a sunflower comes out of this? Really?' 'Really. But not today.' They filled the old can with water. The ground drank it up with a happy sound. Mateo stayed on his knees, staring at the spot where he had put his seed. 'Grandma, nothing is happening.' 'It is happening,' she said. 'Down below, where we cannot see. Look at the sky for a while and breathe. A garden works better when nobody hurries it.' Mateo did as she said. And waiting, for the first time, did not seem so silly to him.

The days turned into a lovely routine. Get up early, do the watering, look. Water the beds, look, wait. Everywhere they went they were followed by Grandma's cat. Nube slept in the only square of shade, with his tail hanging off a flowerpot. Inside the old sprinkling can lived a frog. It was green and small, and it jumped out every time Lucía lifted the can; the two of them would get a fright and then a laugh. One morning, Lucía shouted so loudly that Grandma came out of the kitchen with a spoon in her hand. 'It is here! It is here!' There in the soil was a thin green thread, bent over like an elbow, pushing upward. Mateo crouched down until his nose was one finger away from the ground. 'That is my sunflower,' he said, and his voice trembled a little. 'That is your patience,' said Grandma. 'The sunflower is only the way it says hello to you.' That night, Mateo fell asleep thinking about the things that grow while you sleep.

In the middle of August, the heat grew heavy and the sky changed colour. First came a different breeze, one that bent all the branches to the same side. Then came the smell of rain. And then, right over the house, rolled a huge clap of thunder. The kitchen windows shook. It rained as if the sky had tipped over a giant bucket. The children watched through the glass with their hands resting on it, cold as ice. Out in the yard, a flowerpot fell over with a dull thud. 'The garden!' shouted Mateo. 'Nobody goes out in a storm,' said Grandma, firm and calm, hugging them both. 'The rain is part of the garden too. We will look tomorrow.' It was the longest night of the summer. Lucía fell asleep against Grandma's shoulder, but Mateo listened to every single drop, imagining his green thread out there, all alone, holding up against the water with all its small strength.

Dawn came clean and quiet. As soon as the rain stopped, the three of them went through the blue door in pyjamas and boots. The garden was a mess. Where the path used to run there was now a huge puddle. The new flowers were lying down in the mud, and the broken flowerpot had spilled its soil everywhere. Mateo felt like crying. But Grandma was already on her knees. 'This one did not break, look. It only fell over.' With a stick and a piece of string she tied a bent stem and left it standing again. Lucía made channels with her hands so the water could run away. Mateo lifted the fallen plants one by one, slowly, the way you lift somebody who has fallen asleep. They worked all morning, with mud up to their elbows, and the sun dried their backs. Out of the ten sunflowers, eight were still alive. When they finished, in over the wall flew a fat bee. It circled the flowers slowly, as if it had come to inspect the work. 'Eight,' said Mateo, surprised. 'Eight is a lot.'

On the last Sunday of the holidays, the garden was not the same anymore, and neither were they. Eight tall sunflowers looked at the sun like curious faces. There were white daisies beside the fountain, which now held real water, and the ivy no longer hid the way in: Grandma had left it open on purpose. When evening fell, they carried out three chairs and a blanket. The air smelled of jasmine. An owl asked something from the walnut tree and nobody knew how to answer it. Above them, among the first stars, rose the moon. 'Grandma,' said Mateo, yawning, 'I know what the secret of the garden is.' 'What is it?' 'That you must not hurry it. You have to stay.' Grandma stroked his hair and said nothing at all, because sometimes silence is the best answer. A little while later, the two of them were fast asleep. Under the blanket they breathed slowly, with the smell of earth on their hands and a whole summer tucked away in their chests.
